It’s no secret that major tech companies are pouring resources into mobile apps, but at what cost? The web clients of platforms like Instagram and Reddit are crumbling under neglect, and the evidence is painfully clear. Take Instagram’s web client, for instance. These aren’t minor inconveniences—they’re symptoms of a deeper issue. The causal chain is straightforward: reduced investment in web client development leads to accumulated technical debt, which in turn degrades functionality and frustrates users.

Define the feature/specs

AI tests it

The dev never really looks at the code or tries to understand what AI did.

My coding agent can edit files, run tests, and keep working without me. The harder question is whether it is still working toward the right thing.
Suppose I ask for a configuration parser that rejects unknown settings. The agent decides to accept them instead. It can implement that decision perfectly, write tests for it, and announce success. The code works; the requirement was lost.

articles.author: Ahmed Omeiza
articles.description:
When you write C# code, you create variables, objects, method calls, and data structures.
But where does all that data actually go?
The answer usually comes down to two areas of memory: the stack and the heap.
Understanding the difference helps you reason about memory usage, object lifetime, performance, and garbage collection in .NET.
The stack is used primarily for managing method calls and their associated data.
When a method is called, a stack frame is created. When the method returns, that frame is removed.
For example:
void Calculate()
{
    int number = 10;
    int result = number * 2;
}

The method's execution data is associated with its stack frame.
The stack is fast because memory is managed in a predictable last-in, first-out (LIFO) manner.
Think of it like a stack of plates:
Th…
articles.title: Stack vs Heap in .NET: Where Does Your Data Actually Live?
